title: King Lavana's dream and the seer
hookLine: a king lives a whole hard lifetime in a magician's spell, then wakes on his throne
carry: the seer is not the thoughts it sees
tomorrow: how many ways can a mind turn?
last: YOGA IS THE STILLING OF THE MIND.

cards: Hindus tell a story from the Yoga Vasishtha, a long book of teachings the sage Vasishtha gives to young Rama. King Lavana is sitting in court when a magician walks in and waves a bundle of peacock feathers.
The king goes still on his throne. And inside his mind, a whole life begins.

teach.h: A WHOLE LIFE, ON THE THRONE.
teach.b: He rides off on a horse into a wilderness and is lost. He marries a woman from a poor forest village, has children, and grows old in hardship. A famine comes, and his children are starving.

And then he jolts awake, on his throne, in front of his court, and only a short while has passed. A whole life, and he was sitting there the entire time. Patanjali's next two sutras are about that moment of waking.

teach.h: THE SEER RESTS IN ITS OWN FORM.
teach.b: Then the seer rests in its own form. Then: once the turnings are stilled. Drashtri, the seer: pure awareness, which Patanjali also calls purusha.
When the whirling stops, nothing is lost. The seer is left as it always was.

teach.h: OTHERWISE, IT SEEMS TO BE THE TURNINGS.
teach.b: Sutra 1.4 covers the rest of the time: otherwise, the seer seems to take the form of the turnings. That's Lavana in the forest. Fear rises, and awareness seems to become fear.
A worry spins, and awareness seems to be the worry. The commentators say the seer never really changes; it only looks that way.
Here Patanjali leans on an older school, Samkhya, which separates purusha, the seer, from prakriti, everything that changes, the mind included. The mind is the screen.
The Vedanta schools, the Yoga Vasishtha among them, describe the seer in their own terms, and many Hindu teachers call it the sakshi, the witness.
But on this point they meet: the one who sees is not the passing thoughts it sees.
That's what many Hindus who meditate are doing when they sit with closed eyes: not chasing the thoughts, resting as the one who watches them.

how: In Patanjali's yoga, practitioners learn to witness the mind's movements rather than become them, and many Hindu teachers describe meditation as resting as the witness, sakshi, behind thought.

o: the mind's eye that pictures things
a vision of the future seen in meditation
pure awareness that watches the mind

p: its own form, its true nature

s: in Patanjali's system the seer is the mind
the mind belongs to changing nature. the seer, purusha, is the awareness that sees it.
sutra 1.4 says the seer seems to take the form of the turnings
at other times, it looks as if awareness has become the thought.
in the Yoga Vasishtha, King Lavana lives a whole life in a magician's spell without leaving his throne
he wakes in his court a short while later. Vedanta teachers tell it to show the mind's world isn't the seer.

games.q: a wave of anger rises while you sit. according to sutra 1.4, what is happening?
o: awareness only seems to take the shape of the anger, a turning of the mind.
the anger proves the practice failed.
games.why: otherwise, the seer seems to take the form of the turnings. it never really changes: teachers often compare it to the moon on rippling water, which only looks broken.

practice: Let thoughts come, and notice each one the way you'd notice a scene on a screen: there's a plan, there's a memory, there's a worry.
Then lean your attention slightly back toward the one who is noticing, without trying to find or describe it, the way Lavana woke and found himself on the throne he'd never left.

wordCard.voice: Drashtri, the seer, pure awareness. Sutra 1.3: when the mind's turnings are stilled, the seer abides in its own true form.

orig.note: Sanskrit draṣṭṛ: the seer. in the Yoga Sutras, pure awareness, also called purusha.

carryVoice: Your line: the seer is not the thoughts it sees. Lavana was on his throne the whole time. Day four hundred thirty-one.
